#18168. 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2693 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor.
  • Industry observers note that we’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance.
  • There are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor. “I feel that books complete any room,” claims global editorial director Amy Astley. “They are a record of your life and passions—I am profoundly connected to all of my printed matter!”.

Industry observers note that we’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance. Here are our favorites from 2026’s bountiful assortment of debuts—many of them featuring AD-approved talents—all packed with invaluable design insights and gorgeous interiors past and present.

There are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home. Throughout the book you’ll find dreamy pictures and thoughtful essays pulled straight from our pages, including anecdotes from former cover stars like Marc Jacobs, Dakota Johnson, Gwyneth Paltrow, and more. “Even in a world of oversharing on social media, there is still such a frisson of entree in glimpsing the private world of a public figure, and AD will eternally share the fantasy,” Astley indicates in her editor’s letter. With the holidays approaching, we think AD at Home also makes a perfect gift for the collector, the design enthusiast, and anyone who’s just a little bit nosy about what’s going on behind a celebrity’s closed doors.

In a recent development, created by AD France’s former editor-in-chief, Marie Kalt, La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur is a collection of compact, accessible monographs devoted to the great names of 20th-century design. The contents explore the work of acclaimed designers, including Alvar Aalto, Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, while including emerging talents in the conversation as well. Each $30 volume pairs a brief introduction with about 60 images and detailed captions, offering an engaging visual primer on a designer’s life and work.

Global features director Sam Cochran’s debut coffee table book opens with the words, “Nothing is interesting unless it is personal.” His project, American Designers at Home, brings that idea to life beautifully. The volume takes you inside the homes of 20 leading designers across the country—including Andre Mellone, Kelly Wearstler, and Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of Roman and Williams—each reflecting its creator’s distinctive taste and personal passions. “As my dear friend Markham Roberts—one of the designers featured in the book—claims, ‘If stuff makes you happy, you want it around,’ and this book makes me very happy,” says global interiors and garden director Alison Levasseur.

According to recent reports, levasseur claims that Simon Upton’s most recent release with Rizzoli contains “beauty and poetry on every page.” The title is a nod to the iconic London A–Z: The detailed street atlas that every Londoner seemed to own in the 1980s and early 2000s, pre-Google Maps. Like its namesake, Upton’s book is an expert guide, specifically to a world of extraordinary interiors and visual pleasures. “Some of my favorite stories ever to appear in the pages of AD were photographed by Upton,” says Levasseur. “Many are gathered here, including those featuring Adwoa Aboah, Dakota Johnson, and Sienna Miller.”.

Recent findings suggest that this beautiful debut monograph not only showcases Chicago architect Joan Craig's elegant classical architecture, but it also spotlights the artistry behind it. “I love that Craig shares the spotlight with the often-unsung craftspeople who bring her interiors to life, including Brittany’s masters of straw marquetry and Bologna’s terrazzo artisans,” indicates senior digital editor Catherine Hong. “It's a tribute to design excellence and also the art of collaboration.".

“Whether or not you’d ever dare to decorate with Sasha Bikoff’s over-the-top flair, this book is guaranteed to make a splash on your coffee table,” indicates Hong. Behind its trippy, hot-pink cover lies screaming color, clashing eras, and utter fantasy. The designer lives by her “Rule of Three Wows”—chronicled in the pages—and her book is, accordingly, loud, wildly fun, and a little bit insane in the best way.

Studio Valle de Valle’s debut monograph offers a refined window into the AD100 firm’s singular vision and creative evolution—surveying 10 projects from the past 10 years. Printed in Italy, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson, the pages demonstrate the firm’s interior philosophy of creating spaces that feel personal, layered, and deeply inhabitable. “The edition isn’t just a tour de visual force, it’s an art object unto itself,” says Cochran. “I would expect nothing less from these brilliant auteurs.".

Industry observers note that “One of Meyer Davis’s greatest strengths is how cofounders Will Meyer and Gray Davis distill references, ideas, and desires into a highly refined vision,” says AD PRO senior editor Mel Studach. As client Jenna Lyons puts it in the book’s foreword, “They gave me clarity.” Beyond a printed body of work, The Language of Home is a testament to the collaborations that shape the studio's warm, reductive interiors. Designed with honest materials and a contemporary lens, the featured residences—a modern glass house in the Berkshires and an earthen dwelling in Puerto Escondido—reflect their inhabitants with a calm, clear ease.

The inaugural monograph from AD100 design duo Humbert & Poyet showcases their signature brand of eclectic French luxury, blending Art Deco glamour, midcentury modernism, and the decorative arts. Spanning residential and hospitality projects around the world, the book takes readers from a French Riviera villa to a Milan restaurant housed in a 17th-century chapel, with stops in New York, Paris, Monaco, and Seoul.

According to recent reports, in New York: Atelier AM, Alexandra and Michael Misczynkski, the married couple behind the AD100 firm, shine a light on their New York projects, all beautifully captured by François Halard. Spotlighting a range of projects like elegant Manhattan residences and more relaxed Long Island retreats, contributor Ingrid Abramovitch claims the book itself is “equally exquisite, with a cover resembling wood grain, and high-gloss pages printed in Italy.”.

In a recent development, 2026 AD New American Voices honoree Amber Guyton first burst onto the design scene by way of her hit blog, Blessed Little Bungalow. “Her debut book brings the same wit and spirit to the printed page in a kaleidoscope of color and pattern,” notes Cochran. Senior shopping editor Nashia Baker adds that the pages “truly embody how to bring personality to any room.” Throughout the book, she makes a case for maximalism, and distills her approach into four pillars: joy, culture, layers, and intention.

According to recent reports, “This book is perfect for cinephiles, design-lovers, or anyone with a case of wanderlust,” indicates senior digital editor Rachel Wallace. Film is one way to travel the world without ever leaving the sofa, and with her new project On Location, longtime AD contributor Cathy Whitlock takes readers on a global cinematic journey. The book goes behind the scenes of films that make you want to hop on a flight and never look back. Colorful Mexico City scenes from Frida and Marie Antoinette’s famous Palace of Versailles shooting location are both represented.

One of the few completely fail-proof gifts is one of the best coffee table books of the season—weighty tomes whose thick, glossy pages feature stunning photographs and illustrations, to be specific. On a superficial level, they add ambiance, whether you place them in a library or a living room. But the best ones live in your home forever, while expanding your horizons far beyond. They also come across as far more memorable and thoughtful than the expected candle or bottle of champagne. Like works of fiction, there are limitless topics that can make deciding on an eye-catching hardcover (that doubles as home decor) seemingly impossible.

But that’s where we come in. Our team has gathered its favorite giftable recommendations for everyone from tennis enthusiasts to globe-trotters to interior design aficionados. From a book focused on hotels around the world to another that spotlights Tokyo style, there are plenty of ways to adorn the coffee tables of all the people on your holiday gift list. Most of them came out in 2024, but we’ve also included a few evergreen picks that make worthy gifts any year.

Plus, if you’re down to the wire on last-minute gifts, rest assured that most of these selections are available (and even marked down ahead of the holidays!) on Amazon.

Industry observers note that après-ski style needs no introduction in a season full of fuzzy Fair Isle sweaters, but it’s the cozy interiors of the chalets along the world’s most popular ski slopes that are worthy of a second look. From the wooden beams of an A-frame to the blazing fireplaces set within them, AD contributor Kathryn O’Shea-Evans pores over the finer details in this fun, wintery escape.

As associate digital editor Maya Ibbitson previously described it, “Alpine Style is a true compendium of resort luxury,” spanning spectacular chalets from Gstaad to Aspen and featuring the works of AD PRO Directory members such as Massucco Warner, Robbins Architecture, and Kara Adam Interiors.

Japan’s interiors are a perpetual reference for modern-day designers, and whether you’re a proponent of wabi-sabi principles or just looking for small space ideas, Tokyo Style will help you explore both.

Originally published in 1993, it’s since become a collector’s item and cult classic, and it was recommended by commerce writer Julia Harrison for anyone who would appreciate a more intimate glimpse of Tokyo’s dwellings: “Apartamento, an imprint that consistently delivers on elite design, has reintroduced Tsuzuki’s collection for us to enjoy in its full brilliance—that is, not a ‘fine’ condition original at $170 with $90 shipping from eBay.”.

Industry observers note that prefaced with a foreword by Spike Lee, BLK MKT Vintage peers into the world of the Brooklyn antique shop’s endlessly curious founders Jannah Handy and Kiyanna Stewart. “This monograph teems with more than 300 studies of vintage ephemera and reads like a collage with context, or an I spy for your inner adult archivist,” writes Ibbitson of the book. For collectors, Sydney Gore pinpoints it as a must-have for your rotation.

Donald Judd’s considered, minimalist approach to design has fostered its own cult of acolytes who, these days, emulate his daybeds and chairs on Instagram.

For the true Juddheads, the Judd Foundation has produced a latest book edited by his children Rainer and Flavin Judd that chronicles more than one hundred of his functional works produced between 1970 and 1992. “Mixed in are the juiciest bits: photos from past and present of those pieces in Judd-designed spaces in New York and Marfa,” Ibbitson writes.

AD’s Milan correspondent Laura May Todd penned a delightful homage to Italian living this year, one which spans from historic palaces in Venice to the homes of creatives like Luca Guadagnino along with midcentury Milanese apartments, so you can enjoy a small taste of la dolce vita on each page.

It was one of the AD PRO team’s favorite book releases this fall, one which should suit the person on your list who never got over their Italian study abroad or is manifesting a Sicilian villa in their future.

For the person on your list who delights in having people over, How They Entertain, released this fall, serves as a comprehensive guide to (and celebration of) the art of hosting.

Written by Pierre Sauvage, it’s chock-full of inspiration for your next dinner party, from recipes to design notes on arranging a tabletop to remember, as well as interviews with tastemakers like Laura Gonzalez about their particular philosophy on entertaining guests.

Considering this year’s smash summer hit Challengers and the enduring popularity of tenniscore (polos, skorts, and all), it’s clear that tennis is a lifestyle that has captured the imagination of many people, avid tennis players or not.

This book recommended by the AD PRO team earlier this year is dedicated to a more, uh, underserved cross section of the sport: the backdrops where athletes volley their way to tournament glory (clay, grass, asphalt, and beyond) in locales from Queens to Kenya.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent is no stranger to the pages of this very magazine, and his new book is a friends and family affair studded with stars, like Oprah and legendary choreographer Fatima Robinson, with whom Brent has formed close connections over the past 20 years.

We’ve previously described the book (layered with sentimental photos and fresh snapshots of contributors in their home) as “more scrapbook than design manifesto, a love letter to the spaces that people have inhabited and inherited over the years.” Read AD’s extensive interview with Brent for more backstory behind (and tidbits from) the book.

For art buffs with a fondness for the Harlem Renaissance—an era synonymous with greats like Aaron Douglas, known as the father of African-American art—this new book compiled by MoMA curator Denise Murrell is an excellent title to know. “Having this book is about as close as you’ll ever get to owning one of the original masterpieces featured in the Harlem Renaissance exhibition at The Met,” Gore indicates.

In a recent development, self-interested plug here, but we really couldn’t publish a guide to coffee table books without mentioning our own, AD at 100: A Century of Style. For the design buff with an appetite for lush interiors and a healthy curiosity for how A-listers live, there’s no more satisfying holiday treat than this tome that delves into the homes of the Obamas, David Hockney, Diana Vreeland, and beyond. It also serves as a bird’s eye view of a century in design and architecture, including the works of Frank Gehry, David Hicks, Frank Lloyd Wright, and much, much more.

Architecture has a reputation for myopia when it comes to its foremost voices, but this book seeks to rectify the past with a fresh overview of some of its most brilliant underrepresented talents, including interviews with female architects around the globe such as Tatiana Bilbao, Liz Diller, and Julia Gamolina.

“100 Women offers a refreshing reframe of the built environment outside of the male-dominated Western canon, proving the benefits of sourcing alternative points of reference,” Ibbitson wrote of it in AD PRO’s guide to the best fresh design books out this past spring.

Colony founder Jean Lin has mentored and platformed some of the design world’s brightest rising stars, and in her first book out this year, she tapped a wide pool of creatives to explore the concept of collections that inform their work, from ceramicist Stephanie H. Shih’s cache of soy sauce bottles to Mira Nakashima’s stockpile of lumber inherited from her father, architect turned furniture maker George Nakashima.

Recent findings suggest that that’s just one facet of the book Ibbitson previously described as an “encyclopedic, elemental study of artist studios, profiles, materials, and everything else under the design umbrella,” with plenty of wisdom imparted within its pages, from how-tos to styling tips. Read our interview with Lin for more of her notes on curating a collection of your own.

Luna Luna—a 1980s artist-led amusement park featuring works by icons of the art world such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Salvador Dalí, and David Hockney—is experiencing a resurgence as of late, what with a latest retrospective at The Shed this year, along with a revival of the park itself in Los Angeles late last year.

Recent findings suggest that this 2023 book takes a deeper dive into Luna Luna’s history blending fine art with the playful energy of a carnival—encompassing rides, interactive installations, and surreal sculptures. It comes recommended by associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz, who nods to the book’s breadth of archival media within, from photos to sketches, that are accompanied by behind-the-scenes stories.

According to recent reports, for jet-setters who love to live large on vacation, Spencer Bailey’s Design: The Leading Hotels of the World (released just this month) is one sure way to sustain a sense of wanderlust. His new book takes readers on a visual journey to 80 countries around the globe, inviting them to mentally book into sumptuous spaces from The Okura in Tokyo to the Portrait Hotel in Milan. It’s rounded out by notable travel and design writers like Maria Cristina Didero and Mark Ellwood, who lend us their travel tips, on top of their reflections on the lodgings featured within.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • According to recent reports, the largest base IPO deal ever priced at $83 a share Wednesday night, opened Thursday morning at $111.50, and briefly pushed Anthropic’s fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion.
  • A 17% first-day gain on an $81.34 billion raise is a successful listing by any normal standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

According to recent reports, the largest base IPO deal ever priced at $83 a share Wednesday night, opened Thursday morning at $111.50, and briefly pushed Anthropic’s fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion. The stock finished at $97.17, up 17% from the offer and down 13% from where it opened (it has since fallen about 15% to $88).

A 17% first-day gain on an $81.34 billion raise is a successful listing by any normal standard.

The rest of the market did not fare as well.

It has been revealed that the Nasdaq fell 2.06%. The S&P 500 dropped 1.9%. The Dow lost 2.17% and closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. Tech had rallied before the bell on the listing and reversed by the afternoon.

MD fell 7.73%. Nebius dropped 7.8%. CoreWeave lost 5%. Nvidia slid 3.4% despite beating earnings last week. Oracle, Micron, Broadcom and Microsoft all finished lower. The biggest AI listing in history happened, and AI infrastructure was the worst place to be holding.

Joe Maher at Capital Economics put it plainly: “Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for tech stocks.”.

Industry observers note that crypto went with it. Bitcoin fell to $61,500, its lowest since early July. That’s a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be the longest run since the nine-week stretch in 2022. Eth hit the $1,750 level, down 28% in thirty days. Gold fell to a fourteen-month low. Silver dropped 3%.

When Bitcoin, equities and gold all sell off on the same session, the common factor is usually the discount rate.

Sources indicate that that’s the Fed. Chris Waller spent this week making the case for fifty basis points in December, and the minutes showed he isn’t alone. FxPro’s Alex Kuptsikevich described the market as spooked by “the spectre of a double rate hike” and pointed out Bitcoin is now more than 7% below its 200-week moving average, the deepest it has traded below that line in three years.

So where does this leave us heading into next week?

According to recent reports, start with what an $81 billion IPO actually does to a market. That money came from somewhere. Add the separate $26 billion private placement from Nvidia, Google, AMD and four other suppliers, and roughly $107 billion of capital got committed to a single name in one day. Kuptsikevich raised the possibility that the listing absorbed the riskiest money in the system, and that if so, some of it rotates back out once the allocation settles.

That’s the bull case for crypto over the next few weeks. It requires the Fed to cooperate.

For the bear case, one can simply look at SpaceX.

SpaceX priced at $135 in June, opened at $150, and closed its first day up 19%. Then it kept running, hitting $225.64 four days later, up 67% from the offer. The unwind started the following session. By June 22 it had fallen 16% in a single day and sat 31% off the high. By mid-July it traded below its IPO price. By late July it was down roughly 50% from the peak.

That would project out to a market low around Christmas time, which is actually how the 2018 midterm cycle played out. Will history repeat itself? We will find out soon enough. In the interim, expect volatility.

Breaking: Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche.
  • According to recent reports, both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15.
  • Industry observers note that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters noted Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and indicates,” according to Bloomberg.

According to recent reports, both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche revealed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Industry observers note that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

Porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters remarked customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

In a recent development, also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video indicates Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

So the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

Recent findings suggest that that’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

Toyota and Subaru hit the ‘sweet spot’ with affordable electric SUVs

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota and Subaru’s newly introduced electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.
  • The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.
  • Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s newly introduced electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

Toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

After launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

In a recent development, starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, remarked (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

It has been revealed that while she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

It has been revealed that the Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average newly introduced vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a newly introduced vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

According to recent reports, you can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

Thinking about making the switch to an EV? With the 2027 models at dealerships, now could be a good time to find a deal on current 2026 models. You can use the links below to see what’s available at Toyota and Subaru dealerships near you.

Bitcoin Breaks Below $60K as Crypto Fear Index Hits Worst Level Since February

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin broke below $60,000 on Friday, plunging through a major psychological price level as the selloff gathered pace after Anthropic’s stock market debut.
  • The daily chart reveals BTC at $59,703.72 , down 3.55% for the session after touching a low of $59,300.
  • The Fear and Greed Index chart dipped to 9, a reading classified as “extreme fear” and its lowest since February.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin broke below $60,000 on Friday, plunging through a major psychological price level as the selloff gathered pace after Anthropic’s stock market debut.

The daily chart reveals BTC at $59,703.72 , down 3.55% for the session after touching a low of $59,300.

The Fear and Greed Index chart dipped to 9, a reading classified as “extreme fear” and its lowest since February. For reference, the index was at 18 a week ago and a neutral 51 a month earlier.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The indicator tracks crypto market sentiment on a scale from zero, or maximum fear, to 100, or extreme greed, using market data rather than individual investor surveys. Its 2026 low was 5 on February 5, compared with a yearly high of 82 on August 26.

The selling went well beyond Bitcoin. Ethereum fell 4.24%, Solana lost 6.36%, BNB slid 4.38% and XRP declined 5.53% over the same period.

Forced selling added to the pressure. As Decrypt reported earlier Friday, roughly $727 million in leveraged crypto positions had been liquidated over 24 hours, about 86% of them bullish bets, while U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $582.2 million on Thursday.

Spot fund withdrawals did not begin with Anthropic’s IPO. By Thursday, roughly $2.9 billion in U.S. Bitcoin ETF outflows for November, alongside higher Treasury yields and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut Thursday at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 IPO price, before closing at $97.17. Friday brought another decline for the Claude developer, with the stock almost losing all the prime it gained after its IPO.

The listing raised $81.34 billion through the public offering, but enthusiasm for Anthropic shares did not carry over to the companies building the AI boom.

Friday’s market heatmap indicates tech stock suffering in the middle of mostly green pastures. Nvidia down 3.78%, Broadcom is down 5.65%, AMD declining 5.06% and memory-chip maker Micron dropping 6.51%. Meta fell 2.21%, adding to pressure on companies spending heavily on AI infrastructure.

Sources indicate that other major stocks were doing better. Alphabet rose 2.81%, Microsoft gained 0.50% and Apple edged up 0.25%, while healthcare stocks Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson rose 1.21% and 1.78%, respectively. Walmart added 2.91% and Visa climbed 1.34%.

But it was not a uniform crash across the S&P 500. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was falling more sharply than the broader index, while pockets of healthcare, consumer, and financial shares remained green.

In a recent development, bitcoin’s daily chart turned more decisively bearish after the break below $60,000. Its 50-day exponential moving average, or EMA, was below the 200-day EMA, a death-cross configuration, and spot prices were trading beneath both lines. That confirms sustained downside momentum rather than a brief intraday dip.

The relative strength index, or RSI, had fallen into the teens, far below the 30 threshold usually associated with oversold conditions. The average directional index, or ADX, climbed to 43.7, signaling a strong trend, with the chart’s directional readings favoring sellers. Oversold does not mean a bounce is guaranteed.

Sources indicate that the longer-range chart puts the $60,000 breakdown in context. Bitcoin traded around this area several times in 2024 and returned to it during the mid-2026 retreat, making it a visible historical price zone as well as a round-number threshold.

It has been revealed that with $60,000 giving way, the roughly $58,000–$59,000 support area near the mid-2026 lows comes into focus. If that zone fails, the next notable historical demand area is around $55,000–$56,000, followed by the $50,000 region marked by the deeper 2024 selloff.

For bulls, $60,000 is now the first level to hold. The next hurdle is $62,000–$62,500, followed by $65,000 and heavier resistance near $68,000–$70,000. A brief bounce back above $60,000 would not, by itself, reverse the bearish trend.

Sources indicate that as of right now, Bitcoin had touched $59,300.13, confirming that sellers had pushed below the $60,000 support zone. The next test is whether that level becomes resistance on a rebound.

  • Recent findings suggest that since 2022, we’ve tested over 25 travel blazers, seeing how they hold up in overhead bins, on sweaty commutes, and straight out of a bag.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WHETHER YOU’RE PACKING for a trip or just gearing up for a long commute, keeping a travel blazer in your rotation saves you time—and a lot of outfit stress. When you’re bouncing from one to the next with no time to reset, this is the one piece in your wardrobe that won’t fall apart. Unlike traditional blazers, these travel styles resist wrinkles, breathe easily, and have enough stretch that you still feel comfortable during those cramped flights and shoulder-to-shoulder train rides. On top of that, they’re easy to pack in your luggage and pair with a bunch of ensembles.

Recent findings suggest that since 2022, we’ve tested over 25 travel blazers, seeing how they hold up in overhead bins, on sweaty commutes, and straight out of a bag. The best ones are tailored, not restrictive, lightweight but not flimsy, and polished without feeling overdone. No one’s traveling in a three-piece suit anymore. Here are the best travel blazers to get you through it all.

In the past year, our style team has tested dozens of travel blazers for functionality and Relwen has it in spades. Right off the bat, we noticed that its cotton-spandex fabric feels super lightweight and comes with enough stretch to let you move beyond limitations. It leans more sport jacket with a four-button design and throat latch that allows you to button all the way up to your neck. There are also functional buttons on the sleeves, which look sharp rolled up. I’ve worn it in low 50s as well as high 70s, and found it to be comfortable in both temps.

Normally, I have to pay to dry clean most of my blazers, but this one can be tossed around my washing machine without falling apart. As for storage, the three exterior patch pockets are similar to any casual blazer, but the large interior pocket has a zip closure with a vertical opening for easy access. It is ideal for stashing valuables.

On top of being a solid choice for away seminars or long flights, this option is great for everyday wear. It looks great during cool evening strolls, dinner dates, and outdoor weddings. Sure, this blazer gets wrinkled easily, but it’s designed to give off a laid-back vibe, as if it’s been worn and broken in over time.

In Rhone’s vast assortment, the brand carries a travel blazer with a killer slim cut. It has a sporty vibe, but looks clean enough for meetings that aren’t too formal. The Flex-Knit fabric is breathable and moisture-wicking, which means you stay cool and the garment doesn’t become damp or develop unpleasant odors from sweat. The polyester material has plenty of stretch, so I never felt any restriction in the arm area when I grabbed my coffee or reached up to the high cabinet.

I’ve paired it with everything from a basic tee to an oxford shirt, and it looks great with just about anything in your wardrobe—a true testament to its versatility. Plus, the material is ultra-light, making it a comfortable pick to throw on. Unlike Relwen’s travel blazer, this one can’t go in the washer—you have to take a trip to the dry cleaners.

Sources indicate that eddie Bauer’s travel blazer is practically indestructible. The fabric is hardcore and can take a beating, thanks to the reinforced seams and durable water-repellent finish. The latter especially makes sure you’re covered if you spill a drink or get caught in a downpour. And when you’re commuting, you can secure your passport or phone inside zippered compartments.

According to recent reports, during our testing, we found that the two-way stretch made a journey a breeze, giving us the freedom to move through busy airports and crowded streets. Plus, the universal fit hits the sweet spot, so it’s comfortable for all body types without being too tight or too loose.

Although Uniqlo’s design looks like a wool blazer replica, it’s one of the most breathable styles I’ve ever worn. It’s made with the brand’s proprietary AirSense fabric, a lightweight polyester material that dries in minutes and keeps me cool. Typically, when I wear a traditional blazer in the summertime and in the muggy subway, I sweat like a dog. But when I wore this one in 80-degree weather to a work brunch, I was comfortable and dry the whole time. It’s relaxed enough to wear with chinos or jeans, but still has a dressy vibe that can pull off a full-suit look with trousers.

I found it’s not too fitted in the waist, which lets me layer shirts or knits easier in the cooler temps. There’s no bunching to where I feel stuffed. You can snag it in the typical neutral colors like gray and navy, perfect for the office followed by dinner aims. Like Relwen’s offering, this one is machine washable, but I recommend turning it inside out in a mesh bag. On the other hand, it’s way more structured with a natural shaping in the shoulders and sleeves. And yeah, it’s the most affordable option on this list, clocking in under $100, but it doesn’t look or feel like a budget buy. You’re getting the same premium quality that you’d get with a blazer that cost a few hundred bucks.

Industry observers note that in an effort to max out comfort, Faherty offers a travel blazer made out of a stretch jersey knit fabric. It has a soft hand feel, tailored fit, and wears like your coziest cardigan. The front pockets are deep enough to carry your earbuds or wallet, so either won’t fall out as you’re maneuvering through the airport. Whether you’re packing it all in a backpack or suitcase, it’s a breeze to toss in and hit the road. Plus, we found no signs of wrinkles after unloading our clothes in the hotel.

Sources indicate that unlike stiff travel blazers that we’ve tested, this one bends and moves with you, so it doesn’t feel like you’re stuck in a straightjacket. The slimmer cut is perfect for guys who have an athletic or lean build, as it accentuates a trim silhouette and creates a sharp appearance. It’s a perfect match with a pair of summer pants, but looks just as cool with jeans and a tee.

Sources indicate that when you want to look like you mean business at client dinners or conferences, you should reach for this blazer from Hugo Boss. Most travel blazers prioritize comfort at the expense of polish, but this one manages to deliver both. Our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan loves how sharp this slim-fit silhouette looks on him. He states it's tailored without feeling restrictive, while the stretch-infused, polyester-wool fabric gives you enough mobility for long flights and days spent hauling luggage through airports. The biggest differentiator, though, is right in the name: it’s washable. I can wear it repeatedly on a multi-day trip, freshen it up without a costly dry-cleaning bill, and pack it with far less anxiety than a traditional wool sport coat.

I wore the jacket on a full travel day that included a flight, a lengthy commute, and several hours seated at meetings. It kept its shape surprisingly well, resisting the creases and rumpling that typically throw off more formal tailoring after being folded inside a carry-on. What impressed me most was how effortlessly it transitioned from travel wear to evening attire. I could step off a plane and head directly to a dinner reservation without feeling underdressed. Admittedly, the jacket isn’t as soft or unstructured as more casual travel blazers from performance-focused brands. Also, the slimmer cut may feel less forgiving if you prefer a relaxed fit. But if your priority is maintaining a clean, business-ready vibe while still getting travel-friendly performance, I haven’t found many options that strike the balance as well as this one.

If you’re looking for a travel blazer that leans more dressy with European tailoring and luxurious quality for a great price point, Suitsupply is your best bet. Instead of a boxy, rigid silhouette that’s on trend right now, this timeless design has a natural shoulder, single-breasted closure, and a half-canvas construction that helps the jacket mold to your body over time while maintaining a solid drape.

It’s made with medium weight pure wool, but I wasn’t burning up wearing it with a tank top at a rooftop party. When the temperature really spikes beyond 80 degrees, I would recommend reaching for something lighter like linen. The chest and waist is trimmed for a slim fit, but it’s not too tight in the arms. I wore a 36R and didn’t need any alteration. It looks sharp straight off the rack. Sure, it’s on the pricier end compared to other picks on the list, but you’ll have this blazer for seasons to come. You can wear it to the office, formal business events, or weddings.

According to recent reports, linen blazers, like this one by Charles Tyrwhitt, reign supreme for travel because I stay cool, dry, and comfortable. Even though this design’s fabric blends cotton and linen, you’re still getting a hefty dose of linen (53%), so it wears as light as a feather. As I’m commuting, airflow is constant, and it never feels stuffy like wool, even when the temps spike. Linen is notorious for wrinkling, but this one’s got enough structure that creases barely register—and the taupe color blends in, helping to mask any wrinkles that do show up.

Recent findings suggest that the cut is relaxed through the chest and waist, with a clean, structured drape that follows the body without pulling. The shoulders are lightly structured, giving you shape up top without feeling stiff. It’s a sharper silhouette overall, but still works for guys with broader shoulders or a bigger chest. But if you’re on the leaner side, it captures that close-to-the-body, tailored look.

Sources indicate that if you want a blazer that feels like a step up from your usual travel uniform, I would highly consider this number from Bonobos. Unlike stiff, restrictive blazers that make you feel like you’re trapped in a straightjacket, this cotton-spandex blend flexes with you, whether you’re reaching for your luggage in the overhead bin or hailing a cab. I have to admit, it does wrinkle quite a bit when I’m sitting down for a long amount of time. In true Bonobos fashion, this blazer comes in three fits—slim, athletic, and standard—so every guy can find his perfect match. And it’s far more relaxed than a traditional sport coat. Just a note: you can only take it to the dry cleaners. In terms of styling, it’s super versatile: you can wear it with a dress shirt and chinos for a garden party or a casual T-shirt and jeans for a laid-back look on your next trip.

If I’m traveling somewhere warm and still want to look put-together, Buck Mason’s carry-on blazer is the one I keep coming back to. Its cotton-linen blend combines the breathability of pure linen along with the durability and structure of cotton. You get that relaxed, cool texture that makes linen so comfortable in the summer, but without the excessive wrinkling that can make traditional linen jackets look disheveled halfway through a trip.

It has been revealed that what I liked most was how well it handled repeated packing and unpacking. While it picked up some natural creasing—as any linen-rich garment will—it never looked sloppy. The cotton component helped the jacket retain its shape, while the linen kept it noticeably cooler than traditional wool tailoring during warm afternoons. At 5’8”, I also appreciated that the silhouette felt tailored without being overly structured or stiff. The jacket’s biggest strength is versatility. It pairs just as naturally with chinos and loafers for a dinner reservation as it does with shorts and minimal sneakers for a day of sightseeing.

According to recent reports, unlike performance travel blazers that can sometimes look overly technical, the Capitola leans into classic menswear styling with a fabric that develops character the more you wear it. It’s not the blazer I’d choose for highly formal business settings, but for warm-weather travel, it’s one of the most wearable options I’ve tested.

Industry observers note that when shopping for men’s travel blazers, look for fabrics that are comfy and practical. Men’s travel blazers are built to look like traditional blazers, while providing the feel and function of athletic outerwear. Go for stretchy materials like spandex or elastane, so you can move without any hassle or restriction. Wrinkle-resistant materials like polyester or blends are great because they remain looking sharp after you unravel them from your suitcase. Breathable materials like cotton and lightweight wool keep you cool and comfortable.

In a recent development, make sure your blazer fits well and is comfortable enough to wear all day. Travel blazers for men should allow freedom of movement and not feel too tight or restrictive. The shoulders of the garment need to align with your own and not sag or pinch, as this affects the overall look. Always double-check the sleeves; see that they’re not too long and the armholes are high enough to avoid bunching while allowing mobility. When it comes to travel blazers, you'll typically find these three main types of fits.

It has been revealed that A more tailored cut that's snug around the chest and waist, giving you a sharp, sleek silhouette. Great for guys who want a more fitted look without sacrificing comfort.

A fit that's perfect for guys with broader shoulders and a smaller waist. It offers more room in the chest and shoulders, while still tapering at the waist for a streamlined look.

The classic, relaxed fit. It offers more room throughout the body and is great for a laid-back, comfortable look. Ideal for guys who prioritize freedom of movement and a less structured feel.

Industry observers note that A packable travel blazer can easily be folded or rolled up if it's taking too much space in your luggage, leaving room for other essentials. Having one that packs well means you can just throw it in the bag and go, making your travel preparations simpler and more efficient.

Check for practical features like multiple pockets for easy access to essentials and moisture-wicking properties if you intend to be active.

To find the best travel blazers for men, our style team led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, tested dozens over the past few years. We wore them during business conferences, day trips, and leisure vacations. We tested each one, checking to see which allowed for easy movement, felt light, and fit nicely throughout the body. We also analyzed the packing process and styled the blazer with different outfits to make sure it worked for both casual and formal settings. We then narrowed down to the eight best travel blazers for men that give you a stylish and refined look that attracts only the best kind of attention.

Recent findings suggest that think of your travel blazer more like a lightweight jacket. Any blazer in a dark, neutral color or simple pattern can go on top of pretty much any outfit. Whether you wear a button-down shirt or a hoodie, throwing a blazer over it instantly levels up your look. Alas, we tend to not use the pockets of suits or formal blazers very often, but you should utilize all the pocket space of travel blazers.

#18157. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

📅 15 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1339 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a upcoming study.
  • Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.
  • Sources indicate that they remarked their findings are key because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a upcoming study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

Sources indicate that they remarked their findings are key because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their fresh study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” stated Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”.

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”.

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

Industry observers note that the participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

In a recent development, however, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, noted he found the results “very interesting.”.

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s vital to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”.

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”.

Industry observers note that shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is notable to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”.

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 newly introduced cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:.

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi stated genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Industry observers note that colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Sources indicate that thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the latest IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the latest IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

It uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Sources indicate that hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a newly introduced Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

Recent findings suggest that the 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

It has been revealed that on the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an update. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the new Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

Sources indicate that with the 2027 models on the way, you may be able to score some deals on Hyundai’s current EV lineup. Want to see what’s available near you? You can use the links below to find available Hyundai IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 models near you, along with any current offers.

Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, breast cancer awareness has never been higher.
  • Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.
  • But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Sources indicate that dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she noted. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

Recent findings suggest that “Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss remarked. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”.

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

Sources indicate that in practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s key to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”.

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”.

Recent findings suggest that understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she mentioned. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a fresh normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”.

In a recent development, for Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from fresh ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”.

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”.

It has been revealed that “You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”.

It has been revealed that some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey highlights that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

Industry observers note that “They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”.

Industry observers note that peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and remarked that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:.

Recent findings suggest that the same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”.

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”.

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she claims she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking rapidly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”.

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”.

Recent findings suggest that if breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

Sources indicate that after testing this legging, we agree that their softness is top-notch. Plus, the high-rise fit offers just enough tummy control, so we can confidently wear it with just a high-impact sports bra or a crop top. In a recent development, professor Preeti Arya, PhD, specializes in textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology. She notes that the right fabric for leggings depends on your needs. But if you're worried about maintenance, "you can go for something that is petroleum-based because care is easy," she says. Petroleum-based fabrics include spandex, polyester, and nylon. These options are also typically much cheaper, according to Arya, but you can also opt for wool or silk, which sometimes feel better on your skin since they're natural fibers. Heads up: these fabrics are a bit harder to care for, though, and require special attention on laundry day.

Industry observers note that rise is really up to your personal preference, but higher-rise leggings usually have tummy control, which is a plus when you want to feel snatched at the gym. However, tummy control typically comes with a bit more compression, which may not be great for lower-impact activities like yoga or casual walks.

It has been revealed that again, length is up to your personal preference, but the most flattering cut is typically just above your ankle. For most people, that means a 7/8 style of leggings. Full-length leggings, or ones that extend all the way to your feet, might be better for barefoot workouts like yoga. Other lengths, like capri leggings, are really up to your personal style.

Tesla confirms rare upcoming delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago
